groups.text: Two credits hit one account at once: plus fifty and plus thirty.
Each one reads the balance, converts with an FX call that suspends, then writes.
A common fix is to confine them to one thread, with a view like limitedParallelism(one).
Is that enough?
A reads one hundred and suspends in the FX call.
The thread is free, so B runs, and reads one hundred too.
A writes one hundred fifty.
Then B writes one hundred thirty, right over it.
A's credit is lost.
One thread keeps others out only between suspensions.
A suspension in the middle lets the next coroutine in.
A Mutex holds across the suspension.
A takes the lock, reads, and suspends still holding it.
B asks for the lock and suspends, holding no thread.
A writes one hundred fifty and releases the lock.
Then B reads one hundred fifty, and writes one hundred eighty.
Or keep the view, and move the suspension out: convert first, then read and write with nothing in between.
The two FX calls even overlap.
Code like this waits a lot, and real waits make tests slow and flaky.
runTest swaps the clock.
Delays on the test dispatcher are skipped, and a virtual clock jumps ahead instead.
currentTime reads zero, one hundred and three hundred, after a few real milliseconds.
Only the test dispatcher's delays are virtual.
A delay on Dispatchers.Default stays real, so inject the dispatcher.
This is Kotlin only.
withLock around the whole sequence, and a test that reads currentTime.
So a one-thread view keeps others out only between suspensions.
A Mutex holds across them.
And runTest jumps over delays on a virtual clock.
Quick check. On a one-thread view, a credit reads and writes the balance with no suspension in between.
Can two credits still lose an update?
